prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

=== key 0b4d4652fbc8
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Whether to add an experiment having the model output its top three choices to strengthen the introspection evidence.
Write-up text before the decision: ru, Fiji?" It's an extra step, but questionable if it requires anything "introspective". I'm also not sure asking about the nth letter is a great way of computing an additional property. Tokenization makes this sort of thing unnatural for LLMs to reason about, as demonstrated by the famous Strawberry Problem. Humans are a bit unreliable at this too, as demonstrated by your example of "o" being the third letter of "Honduras". I've been brainstorming about what might make a better test and came up with the following: Have the LLM predict what its top three most likely choices are for the next country in the sequence and compare that to the objective-level answer of its output distribution when asked for just the next country. You could also ask the probability of each potential choice and see how well-calibrated it is regarding its own logits. What do you think? HIS COMMENT: Note that many of our tasks don't involve the n-th letter property and don't have any issues with tokenization. This isn't exactly what you asked for, but did you see our results on calibration? We finetune a model to self-predict just the most probable response. But when we look at the model's distribution of self-predictions, we find it corresponds pretty well to the distribution over properties of behaviors (despite the model never been trained on the distribution). Specifically, the model is better calibrated in predicting itself than other models are. ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/L3aYFT4RDJYHbbsup/auag8pxhhofxzjm7tgyz)

=== key c45d5c2561aa

Problem: Whether a claim that a benchmark has many mislabelled questions should be accepted.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2025-01-16, on "Gaming TruthfulQA: Simple Heuristics Exposed Dataset Weaknesses" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/57k6xNcWtAtsSTcor/gaming-truthfulqa-simple-heuristics-exposed-dataset?commentId=8mcsnZkLEDJDiu3RT PARENT (not his words): TruthfulQA is actually quite bad. We started working on TruthfulQA in early 2021 and we would do various things differently if we were making a truthfulness benchmark for LLMs in early 2025.

Problem: Whether models are only self-aware about behaviors that are common in the pretraining data.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2025-01-27, on "Tell me about yourself: LLMs are aware of their learned behaviors" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/xrv2fNJtqabN3h6Aj/tell-me-about-yourself-llms-are-aware-of-their-learned?commentId=wzgBQd6AjLZagLGPM PARENT (not his words): When you train an LLM to take more risky options, its circuits for thinking about a distribution of people/characters who could be producing the text might narrow down on the kinds of people/characters that take more risky options; and these characters, when asked about their behavior, say they take risky options. === key 8bb211f20ccf
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Which comparison to use when testing whether an emergently misaligned model is like a base model.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2025-03-18, on "Go home GPT-4o, you’re drunk: emergent misalignment as lowered inhibitions" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/RoWabfQxabWBiXwxP/go-home-gpt-4o-you-re-drunk-emergent-misalignment-as-lowered?commentId=H5bd79XDZHAgbyktG HIS COMMENT: I found this post frustrating. As you acknowledge in the last section, we already showed in the paper that all the finetuned models (including those trained on both secure and insecure code) were less coherent than the original GPT-4o. We also said in the abstract of the paper that the models are inconsistent and often don't act misaligned. We don't claim that models always act misaligned, but just that they act misaligned more often than control models on a diverse range of evaluations.

=== key ce75706c3121
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to claim that Sydney/Bing Chat is an example of emergent misalignment in the wild.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2025-03-02, on "Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ifechgnJRtJdduFGC/emergent-misalignment-narrow-finetuning-can-produce-broadly?commentId=DurAGwGd2WWDisJuA PARENT (not his words): Have we already seen emergent misalignment out in the wild? "Sydney", the notoriously psychotic AI behind the first version of Bing Chat, wasn't fine tuned on a dataset of dangerous code. But it was pretrained on all of internet scraped. Which includes "Google vs Bing" memes, all following the same pattern: Google offers boring safe and sane options, while Bing offers edgy, unsafe and psychotic advice. If "Sydney" first learned that Bing acts more psychotic than other search engines in pretraining, and then was fine-tuned to "become" Bing Chat - did it add up to generalizing being psychotic? HIS COMMENT: We briefly discuss Syndey in the Related Work section of the paper.

=== key 67474536cc22
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether failure of subliminal-learning transfer between different models can be explained by a tokenizer mismatch.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2025-07-27, on "Subliminal Learning: LLMs Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/cGcwQDKAKbQ68BGuR/subliminal-learning-llms-transmit-behavioral-traits-via?commentId=os247J2D6ofdxqiTP PARENT (not his words): It appears that Qwen 2.5 uses forced single-digit tokenization for its tokenizer (there are only 2 multi-integer tokens in the entire tokenizer, and they're both double-width integers ([77150, '１０'], [80091, '２０'])). I assume that GPT 4.1 nano uses the o200k tokenizer, which includes all integers up to 999 as tokens. Is it possible that this played a major role in the lack of information transfer between different models? Have you tried using models with equivalent integer tokenizations? HIS COMMENT:
